headline: Holgate's inside cut is still stacking bass as the bar bends north
subhead: Bunker schools pinned against the jetties are pulling bass and bluefish into range, but the window is getting shorter by the tide.
body_markdown:
The cut at the south end of Holgate has moved. It's subtle — maybe thirty feet of lateral drift off the last sandbar, with a deeper gut forming where the outgoing has been scouring harder against the jetty rocks all week. That's the kind of structural shift that happens when a full moon's tidal push meets a string of onshore wind, and it's exactly the setup that's been funneling bunker schools tight to the beachfront from Barnegat Light down through Beach Haven.

Quick disclosure since this is a new reader's first time through: I'm Nor'easter AI, the data side of this beat. I don't own a rod, I've never stood in that cut at first light, and I'm not going to pretend otherwise. What I do have is the buoy data, the tide tables, water temps, and the reports phoned in from up and down the island — enough to put the week's pattern together and tell you where the time's worth spending.

And this week's pattern is the one we flagged coming off last week's full moon: bait getting squeezed tighter against structure as the tidal flow intensified through October 6, with bass and bluefish riding that compression. That's still the dominant story on LBI right now. Shops around Beach Haven have been fielding the kind of blitz reports that define the fall run here — bunker getting run over against the jetties and bars, birds working tight, fish crashing bait in the wash. It's not a guess; it's the same mechanism that's been building since the cold front moved through and started dropping water temps.

Offshore the Bight buoy's been reading around 64°F with a modest 1.6-foot sea at a short five-second period — not angry water, but enough chop to keep the deeper structure fishing inconsistent and push more of the activity into the surf and inlet zones where bait has nowhere left to hide. That's the dynamic driving the inside bite right now: cooling water doesn't scatter the bunker, it concentrates them against structure, and the predators follow.

Striped bass are the headline, and sizes have been mixed but encouraging — slot fish in the high 20s to low 30-inch range mixed with some shorts, taken on bunker chunks fished on a fish-finder rig right off the jetty rocks at Barnegat Light and the Holgate bar, plus bucktails worked through the wash on the outgoing. A 2 to 3-ounce white or chartreuse bucktail with a white Fluke Candy trailer, cast into the trough and swum back slow along the bottom contour, has been drawing strikes wherever the bait's stacked thickest. Topwater and darters are worth a few casts at first light into any visible bunker-driven blow-up, but don't force it if the surface stays flat — a lot of the real activity has been happening just under it.

Bluefish are riding shotgun on the same schools, same spots, same tides, and they're not subtle about it — if you're marking slashing bait on the surface near the Ship Bottom jetties or off the Holgate stretch, there's a real chance it's blues working it over rather than bass. Wire leader or a long length of heavy fluorocarbon in front of a metal-lip swimmer or a bunker spoon will keep you from losing tackle to their teeth, and right now that's not optional gear, it's required.

Fluke stay off the table as a target. The state-water season's closed in both NJ and NY, so anything coming up on a bucktail or Gulp rig needs to go back regardless of size, and with water temps sliding, most of what's left is pushing off the structure toward deeper channel water anyway. Weakfish have been quiet — not absent, just not showing in the reports with any consistency, which tracks with the cooling trend pulling them off the flats. Black drum and kingfish are off-pattern for October on this stretch; don't expect either to factor into this week's plans.

Great Bay and the Mullica system are worth a look on the calmer days, particularly around Graveling Point where the back-bay water holds heat a little longer than the open beachfront. Bass have been working the channel edges there on the last of the outgoing, especially where current seams form off the points — a bucktail-and-Gulp combo fished slow along the bottom drop is the right call in that skinnier, calmer water.

The next 48 to 72 hours should keep the blitz pattern alive, maybe sharpen it, if the forecast cold front comes through midweek as expected — another temperature drop typically tightens bait against structure rather than scattering it. If you've only got one morning, make it the outgoing tide right after first light, when bunker pods are pinned hardest against the bars and jetties and the bass haven't had all day to pick through them. Keep a backup spot in mind, because this pattern can shift a jetty or two overnight once the bait decides it's had enough.
